# True or false: AI

Prompt injection, evaluations, agents and the EU AI Act. Building with AI changes less than people think, and the parts it does change matter a lot.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 5, Assured 1). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area ai`.

### 1. Telling a model in its system prompt not to reveal certain data is an effective security control.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Prompt injection can override instructions, and the system prompt itself can leak. Assume the system prompt is public. Enforce what the model may see and do in code and permissions.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md)

</details>

### 2. Prompt injection can be fully fixed by choosing a better model.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Prompt injection is LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, and it has no complete fix inside the model. The defences that work sit outside it: least-privilege tools, output handling, approval steps and monitoring. Treat retrieved content as data, never as instructions.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md)

</details>

### 3. Model output should be treated as untrusted input before it reaches SQL, HTML or a shell.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Model output can carry injected instructions or plain wrong content. Validate it against a schema, encode it for the context and use parameterised queries. Never pass it to eval or a shell.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md)

</details>

### 4. If an AI feature looks good in the demo, it is ready for production.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A demo shows a few hand-picked cases, while model output is probabilistic. Build an evaluation set of 100 to 500 labelled examples covering normal, edge and adversarial cases, and agree a pass threshold before launch. Run the evaluations in CI on every change.

Read more: [playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md](../../playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md)

</details>

### 5. Banning all AI tools tends to push staff to personal accounts, which is riskier than approving a few tools with clear data rules.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A ban pushes staff to use unapproved tools with personal accounts, where you have no control at all. Provide approved tools quickly, with clear rules on which data may go into them. Block the rest where you can.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-governance.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-governance.md)

</details>

### 6. You should pin model versions and rerun evaluations before switching to a new one.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Providers change models, and a new version can behave differently on your cases. Pinning stops silent changes from reaching users. Rerun the evaluation suite and compare before you switch.

Read more: [playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md](../../playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md)

</details>

### 7. An AI agent should need human approval before any irreversible action, such as sending a payment.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Excessive agency, LLM06 in the OWASP list, is an agent with more tools or power than the task needs. Give each agent the smallest tool set, read-only by default, with scoped credentials. Require a person to approve actions that cannot be undone.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-application-security.md)

</details>

### 8. An AI pilot with no end date and no success criteria tends to drift on rather than reach a decision.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Pilots without an end date drift on without ever reaching production or stopping. A gate in the AI register, 90 days as a starting point, forces a decision. Move to production, change scope or stop.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-governance.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-governance.md)

</details>

### 9. No part of the EU AI Act applies yet, because the high-risk rules were delayed.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Prohibited practices apply from 2 Feb 2025, together with an AI literacy duty that the 2026 amendment reworded as a duty to take measures to support the development of AI literacy. General-purpose AI model obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025. The 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI mainly moved the high-risk obligations, to 2 Dec 2027 for stand-alone systems and 2 Aug 2028 for systems embedded in regulated products.

Read more: [playbook/ai/ai-governance.md](../../playbook/ai/ai-governance.md)

</details>

### 10. Before building an AI feature, you should compare it with a simpler non-AI approach, such as a rule or a search.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Some problems are solved more cheaply and reliably by a rule or a search. The use case assessment asks for a non-AI baseline for that reason. If AI does not beat it clearly, ship the simpler option.

Read more: [playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md](../../playbook/ai/building-with-ai.md)

</details>
